prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a district court abuses its discretion in denying a 28 U.S.C. 1404(a) transfer where the transferee venue is clearly more convenient.

Cite at least six decisions of the Fifth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**The District Court Abused Its Discretion in Denying Transfer Under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a) Because the Transferee Venue Is Clearly More Convenient.**

Section 1404(a) provides that "[f]or the convenience of parties and witnesses, in the interest of justice, a district court may transfer any civil action to any other district or division where it might have been brought." 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a). The statute exists to prevent waste of "time, energy and money" and to protect litigants, witnesses, and the public from unnecessary inconvenience. *In re Volkswagen AG*, 371 F.3d 201, 203 (5th Cir. 2004). A district court has broad discretion over transfer, and this Court reviews a ruling for abuse of discretion. *Action Indus., Inc. v. U.S. Fid. & Guar. Corp.*, 358 F.3d 337, 340 (5th Cir. 2004). That discretion has limits. It is abused when the court errs in its legal analysis, relies on clearly erroneous facts, or reaches a result that is a clear abuse in light of the § 1404(a) factors. The en banc Court has held that a movant need only show that the transferee forum is "clearly more convenient." *In re Volkswagen of Am., Inc.*, 545 F.3d 304, 315 (5th Cir. 2008) (en banc). The movant does not have to show that the existing forum is clearly inconvenient. Where that showing is made, denial of transfer is reversible. *Id.* at 314–15.

**A. The governing framework.**

The threshold question is whether the case could have been brought in the transferee district. *Id.* at 312. The court then weighs the private-interest factors and the public-interest factors. The private factors are: (1) the relative ease of access to sources of proof; (2) the availability of compulsory process for unwilling witnesses; (3) the cost of attendance for willing witnesses; and (4) all other practical problems that make trial easy, expeditious, and inexpensive. The public factors are: (1) administrative difficulties from court congestion; (2) the local interest in resolving localized disputes at home; (3) the forum's familiarity with the governing law; and (4) avoidance of unnecessary conflict-of-law problems. *Id.* at 315; *In re Horseshoe Entm't*, 337 F.3d 429, 433 (5th Cir. 2003). No factor is dispositive. *Volkswagen II*, 545 F.3d at 315. The plaintiff's choice of forum is not itself a factor. It only places the burden on the movant to show that the transferee forum is clearly more convenient. *Id.* at 314–15 & n.10.

**B. The private-interest factors favor transfer.**

This Court has repeatedly found an abuse of discretion where a district court discounted the location of witnesses and evidence. The Court has stressed that the convenience of witnesses is often the most important factor. Where the witnesses and documents are concentrated in the transferee district, the cost and inconvenience of litigating elsewhere are real and substantial. *Volkswagen I*, 371 F.3d at 204–05; *In re Radmax, Ltd.*, 720 F.3d 285, 288–90 (5th Cir. 2013). Convenience also falls sharply as the distance between the forum and the witnesses grows. *Volkswagen I*, 371 F.3d at 204–05; *Volkswagen II*, 545 F.3d at 317. A court errs when it gives little weight to the location of sources of proof on the theory that modern technology has made the physical location of documents irrelevant. *Volkswagen II*, 545 F.3d at 316. The same is true when it relies on the plaintiff's litigation-driven connections to the chosen forum. *Radmax*, 720 F.3d at 288–89. It also errs when it fails to recognize that the transferee court's subpoena power reaches the non-party witnesses who will testify, while the chosen forum's does not. *Volkswagen II*, 545 F.3d at 316; *In re Rolls Royce Corp.*, 775 F.3d 671, 676–79 (5th Cir. 2014).

Defendant identified the relevant witnesses, their locations, and the substance of their expected testimony. It also showed that the key documents and physical evidence are in the transferee district. [Record cites.] Those showings are the kind of specific proof this Court has required. *See Weber v. PACT XPP Techs., AG*, 811 F.3d 758, 766–67 (5th Cir. 2016). The private factors therefore point toward the transferee forum.

**C. The public-interest factors confirm that result.**

The public factors reinforce the private ones. The transferee district has a local interest in a dispute that arose there, and that interest weighs in favor of trying the case there. *Volkswagen II*, 545 F.3d at 317–18. Jurors in a forum with no meaningful connection to the events should not be burdened with the case. *Volkswagen I*, 371 F.3d at 206. Neutral factors such as court congestion and familiarity with the governing law cannot offset the factors that favor transfer. *Radmax*, 720 F.3d at 290; *Rolls Royce*, 775 F.3d at 679–81. Here, [the claims arose in the transferee district / no operative fact occurred in the chosen forum].

**D. The denial of transfer was a clear abuse of discretion.**

When the private and public factors favor transfer and the only countervailing consideration is the plaintiff's initial choice of forum, denial is a clear abuse of discretion. *Volkswagen II*, 545 F.3d at 314–18; *Horseshoe*, 337 F.3d at 433–34. The district court here [discounted the location of witnesses and evidence / treated the plaintiff's choice as a weighty factor / emphasized speculative judicial-economy considerations]. Each of those errors is of the kind this Court has corrected before. The Court should reverse the order denying transfer and remand with instructions to transfer the case to the transferee district.
